speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: For example, could there be dedicated teams of officers working with specific communities?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: Could pilot programmes be evaluated to test the outcome of such an approach?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: Importantly, would restorative justice principles be integrated into community policing efforts to focus on collaborative problem-solving and repairing harm?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: By shifting focus from solely punitive enforcement to proactive community policing and restorative justice, we can build stronger and more harmonious communities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: To mitigate this risk, I suggest the Ministry consider standardising tenancy agreements to include clear clauses about noise and nuisance standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: Additionally, many owners, especially seniors or those with low literacy levels, may not be aware of their obligations or how to comply with required standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: The stress and anxiety caused by disputes between neighbours can have, sometimes, severe impacts on mental health, with potential long-term consequences if not adequately addressed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: Victims may experience feelings of isolation, fear and helplessness, which can affect not just their wellbeing, but their ability to cope with the situation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: Such cases underscore the potential for neighbour disputes to have serious consequences if not adequately addressed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: Accordingly, I seek clarifications on how the Tribunal and those working within the sector will provide support for victims of neighbour disputes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: Yet, even in a society as cohesive as ours, disputes between neighbours can arise, highlighting that we can always do better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: As we work to address these issues through legislation, let us not forget the ultimate goal: to build a Singapore that is not just lawful, but compassionate, kind and just for all, a country where neighbours can resolve differences with empathy and understanding, where those impacted by disputes are supported with the help they need and where we prioritise not just punishment, but rehabilitation and harmony.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim
text: This Bill is a step towards that vision.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Today, I will focus on four key areas within the Bill, including enforcement of mandatory mediation attendance, expanding the authority of CRU, ensuring accountability in settlements and addressing tenant-related noise nuisances.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One critical challenge is the current voluntary attendance at the CMC, which allows residents to opt out of mediation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This often results in one party refusing to engage, preventing timely dispute resolution and undermining the effectiveness of our community mediation efforts.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If a party refuses to attend mediation and also avoids paying the fine, we need additional consequences, such as escalating penalties or legal actions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This will reinforce the seriousness of mediation directives and uphold their integrity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I urge the Government to strengthen these enforcement mechanisms.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The Bill proposes regulatory powers for CRU to handle issues, like noise and hoarding.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is promising and we should consider expanding CRU's scope to address other prevalent issues in our communities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For instance, privacy concerns arise when residents report neighbours installing CCTVs directed toward their units.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Currently, authorities lack the power to investigate or mandate removal of these cameras within private properties.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Additionally, residents have raised complaints about neighbours throwing harmful substances or smoking in common areas.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Will CRU eventually have the authority to manage these issues or could relevant bodies like HDB or NEA be empowered to investigate and take corrective actions?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Addressing these frequent complaints would ensure CRU is adequately equipped to foster a safe and harmonious environment.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This provides swifter legal recourse if a settlement is breached, which is a positive development.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some mediation agreements involve residents and Government agencies.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In such instances, clarity is needed on the accountabilities by all parties.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Would Government agencies represented also be legally bound to act as per mediation agreement?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If so, officials representing Government agencies must be empowered to execute agreements made during mediation and held accountable to uphold them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This will reinforce trust in the mediation process and ensure all parties fulfill their commitments, avoiding breakdowns that affect residents' confidence in community resolutions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The Bill rightly includes provisions for engaging landlords earlier when tenant-related noise disturbances occur.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A minimal bond could weaken the incentive for landlords to take prompt action on tenant disturbances.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Additionally, requiring landlords and tenants to complete a brief programme on noise and neighbourly behaviour before the tenants move in would promote awareness and prevent future complaints.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In closing, Mdm Deputy Speaker, while the amendments to the Community Disputes Resolution (Amendment) Bill are a step in the right direction, there is room for improvement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: By enhancing mediation attendance enforceability, broadening CRU's regulatory scope, ensuring Government agency accountability and establishing effective deterrents for tenant-related nuisances, we can build a more robust framework for community harmony.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I look forward to continued discussions and refinements that will help us create a peaceful and supportive community for all residents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In high-density urban environments, conflicts between neighbours over issues, such as noise, privacy and shared spaces, are inevitable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While these disputes are not uncommon, some can quickly escalate and disrupt the peace of the community if left unresolved.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, not all disputes need to be settled in the courtroom, which can be costly and time-consuming.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Any adjudicatory outcome will also result in a winner and a loser.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is not the best way to resolve a dispute between neighbours who will likely have to continue living alongside each other after court proceedings are over.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Community Disputes Resolution (Amendment) Bill, therefore, addresses this gap by empowering agencies, such as CMC, to encourage early mediation before conflicts worsen with the help of trained mediators.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Disputing neighbours will also be required to attempt mediation before filing a claim with CDRT, something which I have called for since 2021.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Costs can be awarded to compensate individuals for the time and expenses expended for the CDRT proceedings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Crucially, these enhancements should strengthen, not replace, the ability of the community to resolve its own disputes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am therefore heartened that MCCY, MinLaw and MND have consulted the public extensively through engagement sessions over the past two years on proposed enhancements in the spirit of transparency, open discussion and consensus, and received strong support for a CRU pilot to be set up to investigate and intervene in particularly severe cases of neighbour disputes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The CRU, staffed by CROs experienced in law enforcement and supported by auxiliary police officers, will increase accessibility to mediation and arbitration services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: CROs will exercise regulatory powers appropriately and proportionately to investigate, deter and stop noise and hoarding nuisances to resolve differences early and fairly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Some conflicts are rooted in differing perspectives or culturally complex nuances that require careful consideration and understanding.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This Bill acknowledges the challenge of allowing diverse perspectives to co-exist without undermining the peace and harmony of the broader community by providing a framework to address these complexities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To this end, I would like to take the opportunity to clarify three points with the Minister for Culture, Community, and Youth on the proposed Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, under this Bill, if the person contributing to acts of nuisance is suspected to have a mental health issue contributing to the problem, CROs may apply to the CDRT for an order requiring the individual to undergo formal psychiatric assessment or treatment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: What are the guidelines for the duration of treatment required and what if said individual cannot afford the assessment or treatment required?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, to prevent individuals who face prejudice or bias being unfairly labelled as nuisances, will CROs receive culturally informed training or training on how to approach persons with mental health conditions with sensitivity?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For example, studies have linked hoarding behaviour to experiences with material deprivation and mental disorders, and therefore might be more common among lower-income individuals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Such behaviour may thus be driven by complex psychological, social and economic factors rather than simply a desire to be difficult or irresponsible.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, as the saying goes, "Prevention is better than cure." Besides public education initiatives, neighbours should be encouraged to get to know each other and communicate more frequently as a preventative measure.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Investing in initiatives and infrastructure like neighbourhood events, public seating areas and community gardens can go a long way to encourage neighbours to develop empathy and consideration for one another – what we also sometimes call the "kampung spirit".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: What immediate plans does the Ministry have in this respect?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This Bill represents a forward-thinking approach that supports communities in developing the tools necessary to resolve conflicts amicably while giving mediation more teeth and standing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For the minority of cases that cannot be resolved via community self-help, the enhanced CDMF will also provide a wider range of options to facilitate effective conflict resolution.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These measures will strengthen community bonds by building resilience, harmony and mutual respect.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given our population density and recent trends of more residents working or studying from home, increased neighbourly friction seems inevitable.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given this, an updated and strengthened CDMF is essential.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Having consistently advocated for enhancements to the CDMF over the last four Budget and Committee of Supply debates, I welcome these updated and strengthened measures that provides for faster and more effective relief for residents.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given the expected rise in caseload, may I first seek Minister's clarification on plans to increase the CMC's capacity, so that we can improve both accessibility and quality of services at the CMC and satellite centres?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, apart from ensuring reasonable wait-time, such as mediation services can scale, the high success rate of 80%, could it be maintained or even improved?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, can Minister share in greater detail the criteria for issuing a Mediation Direction that recognises the need for timely intervention, yet allowing sufficient autonomy for parties to resolve disputes organically and acknowledging the unique circumstances and thresholds for each case?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Striking this delicate balance will help preserve neighbourly relations and also avoid overloading CMC.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Where mediation proceeds, so as to improve the weight of outcomes, reduce wastage of resources, as well as to reduce administrative load on parties and agencies; can authorities consider for mediation settlement agreements to be automatically lodged as CDRT orders, instead of by consent, as Minister had suggested earlier, for enhanced enforceability at onset?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister also clarify the mechanisms in place to prevent the abuse of taxpayer-funded CMC services?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If parties who offend or are unable to exercise basic tolerance, can they be made to defray more mediation costs on top of the existing $5 administrative fee?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I share Minister's position that CMCs should not be relied on as the first port of call and in fact rely on the community as the first and primary place to resolve neighbourly disputes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, in encouraging a resolution by parties themselves, will Minister employ further strategies to increase residents' onus and awareness of self-resolution approaches?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: And in recognising that grassroot leaders are often one of the first places to engage in such disputes, can Minister also elaborate on plans to further equip our community, as well as grassroot leaders for them to help ease conflicts at the early stage with proper support and advice?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For this pilot, the CRU has been well calibrated with powers that includes safeguards to proactively tackle complex and recalcitrant cases.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: That said, there is a need to enhance the effectiveness of CRU and other agencies to address the root causes of persistent anti-social behaviour.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: From my experience in the community, underlying reasons could range from mental health issues to religious or superstitious beliefs, or longstanding habits and other socio-economic vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For example, there has been a case of a persistent bird feeder at the new BTO flats at Nee Soon Link, which has resulted in much complaints across the neighbourhood, which has also been covered by the media.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, can the Minister elaborate on how CROs will be adequately equipped to assist in such severe cases, like in the case of the bird feeder, where the authorities and our community appear to be at a loss of what to do next?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Can engagements by the CROs be supplemented, for example, with the expertise of psychologists for earlier and more accurate diagnosis of such behavioural root causes so that appropriate actions can be taken to swiftly prevent repeat offending?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For residents who may require more holistic support beyond psychological issues, such as social, financial or housing aid; can the Minister share if and how CRU will collaborate with other agencies and even religious organisations to avail more comprehensive help, and to monitor their follow-through?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This should ideally extend beyond the CDRT's mandatory treatment orders and HDB's limited set of actions that may have limited effectiveness in tackling the issues.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Specific to the pilot, can the Minister clarify the pilot's success metrics, as well as avenues for residents to provide feedback on the CRU's interventions?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: And if there are earlier signs of success, can scaling of CRU to other townships be accelerated even before the one-year timeframe?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: And if so, can more communities and residents benefit from this initiative?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If there is indeed a second team to be trialed, can the pilot cover selected high severity cases island-wide, rather than a single township, to broaden the pilot's learnings?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is in good implementation, where measures including CDRT orders are made to be holistic in addressing the root causes; and with continuous monitoring of their effectiveness – that our community will experience the benefits of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In the end, these enhancements should strengthen, and not replace the ability of communities to come together to resolve differences as good neighbours.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In my opinion, the true success of this Bill lies not much as in the expanded powers of our agencies; but collectively and fundamentally, in the "kampung" spirit of mutual respect and empathy that has come to define Singapore over the years.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, we can forge harmony amidst diversity.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Harmony within our community is fundamental to Singapore's vibrant and tight-knit social fabric.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given our population density and recent trends of more residents working or studying from home, increased neighbourly friction seems inevitable.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, during the pandemic, public feedback on noise climbed and remains unabated.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that the Government has intervened to clearly propose enhanced measures to the existing laws for resolving community disputes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, these laws are not panacea and our communities should also fulfil their own obligations and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The deleterious consequences of noise pollution on physical and mental health is not trivial.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has been noted that prolonged exposure to disturbing and incessant noise can lead to adverse health outcomes like abnormal perception of loudness and noise, ringing in the ears and even distorted hearing.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Equally worrying, exposure to prolonged noise is also related to a host of psycho-emotional conditions like irritability, frustration, anxiety and stress, and could also lead to sleep disturbance like insomnia.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I empathise with residents who have been suffering from noise nuisance from their neighbours and the surroundings.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my constituency of Ang Mo Kio-Hougang, of all the different noise-nuisance cases I have had to deal with, a particular case dubbed the "Hougang Terror" stands out.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a case that has been surfaced to the highest levels of Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I see Senior Minister of State Sim Ann nodding at me.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has also been featured on social media as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am particularly, personally familiar with the case having been on the ground to try and mediate this, without much success.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Essentially, what started out as a dispute between two neighbours resulted in one neighbour incessantly beating a stick furiously against the wall of his neighbour for hours on end – and by "hours" I mean hours on end – which then led to noise pollution and affected the entire, the entire block, the entire carpark, even the blocks surrounding it.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the pilot is a productive one and we are able to implement this scheme in other townships as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am all for community involvement and for people coming together to try and solve issues as amicably as possible without the need for agencies to get involved, without the need for legislation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I do hope that the Ministries can provide more information on what is deemed to be "failure to resolve the disputes among themselves".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How would the Ministries determine if the complainant has made sufficient efforts to resolve the dispute with the alleged offender?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And what would be examples of evidence that the complainant must submit to CRU to prove his or her case that they have tried but failed to resolve the dispute?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I understand that certain objective criteria must be set so that the investigative and directive powers of the CRU will not be abused, I hope that the bar will not be set too high such that the CRU is inaccessible for most of the complainants.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My second point is regarding how we would manage alleged offenders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was recently reported in the media that an alleged offender who had caused six out of eight units on her level in Punggol to move out, had then relocated to Bukit Merah and is now continuing with her terrorising antics in that new estate.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the relevant authorities consider preventing alleged offenders in well-known cases from relocating to a different housing estate until the matter can be resolved or the authorities are sure that they will not cause further nuisance to their new neighbors after moving in.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe this is important as it ensures that we do not "transfer" a problem from one estate to another, which then brings a new set of issues into what was once, perhaps, a rather peaceful neighbourhood or rather peaceful environment.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, in this regard, I hope the relevant authorities can shed some light on how these alleged offenders can be managed if they have purchased a resale flat elsewhere or, perhaps, are in the queue for a BTO flat.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the authorities also consider requiring all flat owners to sign a letter of undertaking as part of their HDB Flat Eligibility letter application, undertaking that they would refrain from creating noise nuisance or other forms of nuisance for that matter at the point of flat purchase and inform them clearly about the consequences of breaching these undertakings?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some feuds can go on for several years, sometimes involving many family members from both sides.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In some extreme situations, as my example from Hougang I cited earlier, multiple other households get drawn into the feud as collateral damage, and this leads to a largely unpleasant living environment for everyone involved.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I am a firm believer in using more amicable ways to de-escalate any potential community conflict, I am also heartened that the Government is taking this issue seriously and this new legislation will allow us to take recalcitrant offenders to task for the overall benefit of the entire community.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is not the first time that we are talking about dispute resolution within this House.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These range from noise complaints and cooking odours to concerns over shoe racks blocking common corridors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While these issues may seem minor, they can escalate into significant conflicts between neighbours.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is a step in the right direction to address such issues, but I would like to raise some clarifications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do landlords have the level of control that this Bill assumes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Typically, landlords have some influence over tenants through rental agreements, which sometimes include restrictions on certain activities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This implies that landlords may have a role in promoting harmony among residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, when landlords, especially those living abroad or slow to respond, struggle with tenant issues, it can lead to prolonged problems for neighbouring residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should landlords face penalties for circumstances beyond their control and what happens if a landlord is unable or unwilling to engage?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, rental agreements usually focus on rent and maintenance, not managing neighbourly disputes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would create legal ambiguity, especially if landlords lack clear authority over tenant behaviour.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If tenants face repercussions, they may shift blame onto their landlords, especially absentee ones, potentially prolonging disputes and leaving the complainant in limbo.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Before imposing additional responsibilities, I urge the Minister to provide clear guidelines to help landlords understand their obligations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us define what is fair and establish mechanisms that are effective for all parties.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill rightly seeks to empower landlords with clearer guidelines and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, these expectations must be balanced and realistic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Ministry to ensure that landlord obligations are practical and if necessary, to provide resources that facilitate compliance, rather than unintentionally fostering disputes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We understand that hoarding poses public health risks, but it is also a deeply personal issue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What happens after someone's belongings are cleared out?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hoarding behaviour often recurs, making temporary solutions inadequate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without mental health support, such as counselling and follow-ups, this issue is likely to resurface.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must strike a balance between protecting public health and showing empathy towards those struggling with hoarding.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the Ministry consider integrating mental health support into hoarding interventions, perhaps through partnerships with social services?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could provide a more holistic and lasting solution for affected residents and their neighbours.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, this Bill may not fully address disputes occurring in private properties like condominiums.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do the provisions apply in these contexts?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can CROs or ACROs enter private homes to resolve issues?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will Management Corporation Strata Titles (MCSTs) be involved?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will officers need MCST permission to enter and remove hoarded items?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, what are the limits of officers' powers in condominium disputes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can they enforce compliance, or must they rely on MCST cooperation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is important to clarify how this Bill applies to private properties, as condominiums represent a significant portion of Singapore's housing landscape.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the Ministry look into clearer guidelines for disputes in private properties, ensuring officers have the necessary authority while respecting MCST boundaries?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While their authority to issue orders and enter homes may be necessary, we must safeguard against potential overreach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What checks are in place to prevent misuse of these powers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mental health issues, personal struggles and vulnerabilities often complicate matters.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are these officers trained to handle such situations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are they equipped to de-escalate conflicts and identify when professional help is needed?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear, consistent guidelines are needed to ensure fair, informed decision-making.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry consider a framework for CROs that includes rigorous training and guidelines to prevent escalation and maintain community trust?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to emphasise the importance of mediation, particularly under section 13M, which refers to CRO referrals for mediation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have always been a strong advocate for mediation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mediation fosters lasting peace in a way that legal battles cannot achieve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Formal mediation can feel burdensome for many residents, who juggle jobs, family responsibilities and health issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could we enhance accessibility by conducting more sessions in community spaces or offering sessions during evenings and weekends?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear guidelines must be established to prevent stalling tactics and once an agreement is reached, swift enforcement is essential to maintain its effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without the right support, interventions can inadvertently cause harm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Yio Chu Kang, we have a local mediation team composed of volunteer grassroots leaders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This initiative is useful, as having neighbours involved in mediation offers a familiar face and helps track progress.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, while this Bill provides valuable tools, it must empower individuals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Conflict resolution requires neighbours willing to engage in dialogue, approach disputes with understanding and seek common ground.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let this Bill not only police conflicts but also nurture collaboration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let it strengthen our communities' social fabric and foster lasting peace.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This reflects the essence of the Forward Singapore movement to cultivate a kind and cohesive society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have four points of clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the roles and powers of CRO and ACROs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The requirement is that this individual must have suitable training to properly exercise the powers of an ACRO.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share how the powers of a CRO and an ACRO are different?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is considered suitable training for an ACRO and who will provide the training?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The DG may issue a CRO and an ACRO with equipment necessary for them to discharge their duties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister give examples of equipment that might be provided to a CRO or an ACRO?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the protection of monitoring data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Data that is collected for the purpose of community disputes can be highly intrusive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is the reason the Government has given in response to my suggestion, that we use cameras to catch people who are smoking at their windows or balconies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The CRU which carries out the functions of the Act is a multi-agency initiative by MinLaw, MCCY and MND.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that there are at least three Ministries which may use the monitoring data collected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share exactly which Ministries and agencies will have access to the monitoring data obtained by an officer or recorded in any detection and monitoring equipment installed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the period of storage of such data?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will this data be expunged and which agency shall ensure the expungement?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will the agency ensure that the data is expunged across the board by all Ministries and agencies?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on tribunal orders to address hoarding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These powers include disposing things contributing to hoarding, entering into a place of residence to investigate unreasonable interference and seizing items used to cause unreasonable interference.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister explain what it means that an order or power may be carried out with or without the consent of the owner?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is an officer supposed to first attempt to seek consent before taking steps without their consent?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide examples of what would constitute unreasonable interference and clarify if hoarding that does not reach the level of being unsafe or unhygienic may, nonetheless, constitute unreasonable interference?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In situations where the removal or disposal of items are ordered, can the Minister clarify who will bear the costs for such removal or disposal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My fourth and final point is on second-hand smoke in homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will raise this again in hope that we will review our policies to save lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The CRU focuses on neighbourly disputes on noise and hoarding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are important issues which affect someone's quality of life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad we are taking steps to address them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we will put in equal effort to tackle second-hand smoke, which kills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: According to the World Health Organization and the Ministry of Health, there is no safe level of exposure to second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are talking about conditions like coronary heart disease, stroke and lung cancer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Those inhaling second-hand smoke are actually exposed to more chemicals than the smokers themselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sidestream smoke is four times more toxic than the smoke that a smoker inhales from the cigarette.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For the vulnerable, including the elderly and young children, even a little is already too much.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure many colleagues will have the same experience of getting feedback from concerned residents about second-hand smoke in their homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A 2022 survey I conducted highlighted the widespread nature of this problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When their neighbours smoke at balconies and at windows, second-hand smoke enters their homes and they feel helpless about the health risks facing their families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Ang shared with me her family's struggles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her young son suffers from sinus problems and asthma.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Ang's attempts to approach their neighbour to resolve the problem were futile.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her family endures a routine of closing all doors and windows to avoid the smoke whenever the smoker starts smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This daily adjustment comes at the cost of ventilation, fresh air and peace, even in their own home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Then, there is Ms Leu, who attempted to speak amicably with both sets of neighbours, one above and one below, who smoked regularly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Leu's polite attempt and appeals were met with indifference, with one neighbour telling her to "close up all   windows" if she is allergic to smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second-hand smoke poses very real health risks that can be fatal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Those who have sought recourse through the CDRT often run into dead ends too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Zhong and her elderly mother live above a neighbour who smokes persistently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They obtained a CDRT order banning smoking in the neighbour's flat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second-hand smoke continued to infiltrate Ms Zhong's home, severely affecting her mother's health and heart condition and their overall quality of life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Zhong has documented the smoker's impact, reached out to other affected residents and sought enforcement of the order.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, the media reported on the story of a woman whose seizures were triggered by her neighbours' smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She fell unconscious and had to be brought to the hospital in an ambulance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the family had to resort to obtaining a doctor's note stating that the woman's intracranial haemorrhage, which left her with seizures and paralysis, is aggravated by cigarette smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her husband told the media, "My wife is left with only her left brain functioning.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If another blood vessel bursts in her right brain, she will be pronounced dead." No one should have to live in such constant fear.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We faced the same issues of enforcement for noise disputes, which this Bill addresses through its amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we will take second-hand smoke just as seriously.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I am heartened by the keen interest that many Members have shown in this topic as well as the strong encouragement that Members have offered to our fledgling team of officers who will be forming the CRU.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members' candid sharing of cases from their own wards is greatly appreciated and will inform our approach as we roll out the CRU pilot.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Minister Edwin Tong will address the questions on the overall community disputes framework, mediation and CDRT.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Dennis Tan, Mr Faisal Manap, Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Mark Lee and Mr Saktiandi Supaat have raised some questions with regard to who constitute the CROs and ACROs, and also whether their services are chargeable.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We do not intend to appoint volunteers, such as grassroots leaders, to serve as CROs and ACROs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Mark Lee, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Assoc Prof Razwana Begum, Mr Darryl David, Mr Alex Yam and Mr Yip Hon Weng have asked for clarifications regarding the CRU's powers.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In proposing the CRU's powers, we have incorporated feedback from public consultations and various stakeholder engagements.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To assess whether the noise is causing unreasonable interference, CRU will consider various factors, such as the loudness or intensity of the noise; the time of occurrence and the duration; what is reasonably expected to be tolerated in ordinary daily living; the impact of the noise on the neighbours; and whether the noise is caused intentionally, recklessly or negligently.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is because it is not straightforward to set across-the-board thresholds for noise and apply them in all situations.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For example, the ambient baseline differs in different neighbourhoods and at different times of day; and the same noise made during the day, when most people are up and about would impact differently than if it were made in the middle of the night, when most people are resting.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: CRU will exercise these powers with due regard to the severity of the noise disturbance.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr A sent multiple complaints over several months to HDB about noise from his neighbour living upstairs, Mr B.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: HDB officers engaged Mr B as well as surrounding neighbours.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The surrounding neighbours said that they did not hear any noise nuisance from the alleged unit and instead pointed to Mr A's unit.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Later, Mr A admitted to retaliating to the noise he perceived to be coming from Mr B and Mr A's family member staying in the same unit corroborated that Mr A was, in fact, the nuisance maker.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: HDB officers also observed items in Mr A's home that may have been used to cause the noise nuisance.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: And yet, Mr A continues to write in to allege the same noise nuisance against Mr B.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If Mr A persists in his frivolous and vexatious allegations, the DG may direct Mr A not to further make such unfounded complaints.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These powers are important safeguards to avoid residents being subjected to unnecessary investigations for unmeritorious complaints and preserves the CRU's resources for worthy cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To Mr Darryl David's question about the bar for CRU to intervene, and Ms Ng Ling Ling and Ms Hazel Poa's questions on the dismissal of complaints not made in good faith, I would like to assure Members that all cases escalated to CRU will be carefully assessed.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: CRU has been developing, in partnership with the relevant agencies, a framework for severe neighbour noise cases to be escalated for assessment and follow-up.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In general, a case will be considered severe if the noise persists over a period of time, say, several weeks or more and causes distress to neighbours despite attempts by the neighbours to resolve the issue between themselves and assistance by frontline officers.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Cases will be closed or dismissed only after the relevant assessment has been done.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: With regard to Ms Ng Ling Ling's concerns about the privacy of a genuine complainant, because CRU deals with protracted, severe cases escalated by HDB and other frontline agencies, the nuisance maker and the complainant would, usually, already be known to each other.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Nonetheless, if there are law and order risks, frontline agencies, CRU and the Police will closely coordinate and monitor the case and CRU will refer the case to the Police, if necessary.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Genuine complainants who are concerned about harassment may also seek remedies from the Protection from Harassment Court.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Alex Yam asked how CRU would use noise sensors responsibly.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As I mentioned in my opening speech, safeguards have been proposed.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: First, if noise sensors are deployed within residents' homes, this will be done only with consent.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They are intended to support CRO's initial investigation.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For example, to ascertain the timing, direction and intensity of the noise nuisance.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Second, the actual sounds picked up by the sensor will not be available to our officers.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Only processed data, which is, charts and tables that show the direction, timing and intensity of the noise events, will be retained for the purposes of CRU's investigation and any subsequent Court proceedings.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Operationally, we are looking at having all raw data being processed automatically within 48 hours.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As I have mentioned earlier, the processing will be done in Singapore-based servers that only a very small number of authorised MND officers and vendor personnel can access, with all access and activities logged.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is in line with prevailing Government data security policies and guidelines, such as the Public Sector Governance Act and Government Instruction Manuals.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In the event that the Police requests for the noise sensor data for law-and-order reasons, CRU will be obliged under the Criminal Procedure Code, or CPC, to provide whatever raw or processed data that is available at the point of request to the Police to aid their work.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It is in the public interest for the Police to have access to such data.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Police must be able to pursue all available information and leads to bring perpetrators of crime to justice and to protect public safety and security.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In this connection, Mr Dennis Tan had suggested the use of sensor data before mediation.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Our thinking is this: mediation works well when both parties are willing to talk with one another and this involves some acknowledgement that there is noise being made.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Whereas sensors would come in more useful in cases where, perhaps, one party may acknowledge that there is noise but the other party denies it.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In such cases, the sensors will help us make a more objective measurement.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I should also address Mr Dennis Tan's concerns.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Yes, we are sourcing for sufficient units of noise sensors so that CRU can carry out its work effectively and without the parties being involved in cases having to wait too long.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Louis Ng, Assoc Prof Razwana Begum, Mr Mark Lee, Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Derrick Goh, Mr Alex Yam and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the setup of the CRU and how the CROs and the ACROs will be trained to handle cases sensitively and bring in additional professional help when needed.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In addition, a number of them have experience in law enforcement.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They will also undergo training by the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) to identify and support persons with mental health needs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They are qualified security personnel who have undergone basic APO training and have at least one year of experience in carrying out auxiliary police activities around Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They will also be trained by the CRU to perform their roles as ACROs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The ACROs are meant to accompany and assist CROs in the discharge of their functions and to provide physical security.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To this end, they will have a narrower set of powers, under section 13J.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For example, both CROs and ACROs may verbally advise persons to stop certain acts that are causing excessive noise.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Both may also take statements from affected parties.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, only CROs can issue written warnings under section 13I(1).

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: ACROs will also be paired with CROs at all times.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the equipment that may be provided to CROs and ACROs to carry out their duties.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: CROs and ACROs will be provided with equipment to carry out their roles, such as tablet computers and body-worn cameras.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As mentioned, they can also be authorised to deploy noise sensors.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Alex Yam also asked about how residents would identify CROs and ACROs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They will be issued with an authority card and officers must identify themselves in the course of duty.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members of the public can also verify the identity of the officers via the MND website.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As far as practicable, CROs and ACROs will investigate and enforce against severe cases without entering the unit or seizing items.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: When they do need to exercise such powers of entry and seizure, they can do so when pre-conditions have been met and there are also statutory safeguards in place.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For example, under section 13I subsection 1, para m, CROs may only enter a unit to install noise sensors with the consent of the owner or occupier of the unit.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: So, I hope this addresses the concerns that Mr Dennis Tan had raised in the course of his speech.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The DG must also approve the CRO's request to enter a resident's home.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As Members will see, the individual would have been given ample warnings and chances to comply with, and if the individual still does not comply and continues to cause severe noise disturbance to the community, then the CRU will have the necessary powers to intervene and to put a stop to the noise.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Some Members spoke about the compulsory acquisition of flats and had some questions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Darryl David suggested preventing nuisance makers from relocating to another estate until the authorities are certain that they will not cause further nuisance, so that a problem is not transferred from one estate to another.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members would know that compulsory acquisition is already being done in serious cases, where flat owners breach HDB rules.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It stands to reason that in an extreme case where a HDB flat owner persistently and egregiously disturbs the peace of his neighbours despite all measures, such as abatement orders, that compulsory acquisition be also made available as a consequence of last resort.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As with all compulsory acquisition cases, safeguards will be in place.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I should add that I will speak a little bit more about such cases later.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To Ms Hazel Poa's question relating to cases where the root of the issue may lie in a lack of understanding of the law, let me reassure Members that our interactions with residents, both verbal and written, will be conducted in plain and simple language, including in the vernacular, where necessary.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is to ensure that our intentions and the implications of the residents' actions are made clear to them.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To Mr Darryl David's suggestion, we recognise that there are no simple solutions in this complex issue.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Next, Mr Derrick Goh asked about how CRU would collaborate with other agencies and professionals to diagnose and address the underlying root causes of behaviours, such as social or psychological root causes.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For example, there was a case that involved frequent slamming of a front door and gate at a HDB flat which affected neighbours.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It turned out that there was marital strain between the couple living in the flat.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: One party was slamming the door and gate to show displeasure towards the other.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: So, the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) officers were brought in to encourage the couple to try marital counselling.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Going forward, CRU will take a holistic approach to resolving disputes, including bringing in other public agencies and stakeholders with the relevant expertise or referring cases to them, when needed.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members spoke about the approach for cases involving persons with mental health conditions or special needs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For instance, Ms Ng Ling Ling asked how the initial mental health assessments involving persons with mental health conditions will be carried out.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: And Mr Alex Yam asked on how CROs would handle interactions with persons with mental health conditions or special needs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I will address the question in the context of how CRU will approach these cases while Minister Edwin Tong will address questions on CDRT MTOs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We are cognisant of the need to approach such cases sensitively.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: At the same time, we also recognise that persistent noise disturbances can be very disruptive and take a toll on the health and well-being of the wider community too – something which several Members have also spoken about.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Our approach is: first, to address disturbances in the neighbourhood in a timely manner, to maintain a peaceful living environment for all; and second, to support persons with mental health conditions to get the help they need.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This means to facilitate the assessment, confirmation and treatment of the mental health condition.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will approach these cases with care and sensitivity, and manage them differently from other cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: When they come across such cases, they will bring in professionals from agencies, such as the AIC to assist.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: CRU officers will seek to understand the unique challenges faced by these individuals and their caregivers, and work with mental health professionals to refer them for the support needed, even as we address disturbances to the community.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hopefully, with treatment, the resident's condition will improve and the disamenity to the community will be reduced.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As for persons with special needs, very often, these cases call for empathy, encouragement and support, in addition to finding workable solutions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Where the noises create significant impact, despite neighbours making allowances for it and cannot be easily reduced, CRU may need the help of social service agencies, in addition to the person's family members or caregivers, to develop appropriate solutions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Several Members spoke about the approach for hoarding cases and the decluttering order.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Louis Ng and Assoc Prof Razwana asked for details and examples on the decluttering order to address severe hoarding cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked whether there is any recourse for hoarders when faced with a CRU application for a decluttering order.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: He also asked if it is possible for hoarders to be directed to undergo psychiatric treatment.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: And Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if the Ministry could consider integrating mental health support into interventions for hoarding cases, while Dr Syed Harun asked for more info on the state of serious hoarding cases in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Earlier in my opening speech, I talked about grief, trauma, it could be loss, it could be psychological pain.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: There could also be mental health conditions involved, but not always.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: And addressing hoarding behaviour in a sustainable, long-term manner would usually have to involve some very thorough understanding of what the person is trying to balance or address, through keeping items that most people would deem are of very little value.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This may also have to involve a change in the person's routines and also a shift in the person's daily focus.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I think Members would agree that this is not easy to do, even for very highly trained personnel.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: So, we do not view decluttering as an end in itself.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We also acknowledge that entering a person's home to remove their property is highly intrusive, so the decision to do so is not taken lightly.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As mentioned earlier, we take this measure premised on public interest and it is to be used after other regulatory levers have been exhausted, and when efforts by agencies and community partners to obtain the hoarder's cooperation to declutter have failed.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We know that hoarding affects not only the hoarder, but also their neighbours.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Examples where hoarding may constitute unreasonable interference include situations where there are excessive smells or pests.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This can have a severe impact on neighbours and affect the enjoyment of their homes, even if it does not cross the thresholds for agencies, such as NEA, to take enforcement action on.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Where the hoarder has a suspected mental health condition, CROs will work with mental health professionals from relevant agencies and community partners to refer such cases for the appropriate mental health assessment and support.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If the hoarder with the suspected mental health issues refuses assistance or assessment, affected residents can file a CDRT claim and apply to the CDRT for an MTO.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If necessary, the DG of CRU can also apply to the CDRT to seek mandatory treatment for the hoarder after the CDRT has found the hoarder to be causing unreasonable interference to his neighbour.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The MTO process, which Minister Edwin Tong has explained in his opening speech, will apply.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Given the complexity of the issue and the impact of hoarding on the individual, as well as the individual's neighbours, a whole-of-society approach is needed to address the issue in a more holistic and sustainable manner.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This entails Government, social agencies, community groups, grassroots organisations and the private sector coming together to learn from and tap on each other's strengths and capabilities.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In general, advisories to declutter are issued to the hoarder by frontline agencies and Town Councils.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is an existing practice by the Agencies for Hoarding Cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To be clear, grassroots advisers and MPs are not considered to be a person exercising a public official function under these amendments.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This would refer to statutory office holders in agencies, such as the Director-General of Public Health.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: He also asked how feedback from stakeholders in the pilot region will be incorporated.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We also intend to track the extent to which the early issuance of Mediation Directions by frontline officers is effective in encouraging neighbours to attend mediation at the CMC.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Agencies will continue to refine the qualitative and quantitative data points that they track to evaluate the effectiveness of the CRU model.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will also carefully consider feedback from frontline agencies and stakeholders in the pilot town.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Several Members asked about the scope of CRU model and pilot.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In short, Members have urged us to do more, scale faster.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: There have also been questions about whether the CRU can provide 24/7 response or response late in the night.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: From the cases we have been studying, the key to eventual relief and resolution to serious and long-standing noise disputes is not so much having officers appear on the scene right after a report has been made.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Rather, the key lies in moving more cases through the mediation and CDRT processes, and investigations leading to the issuance of formal warnings, abatement orders and if necessary, MTOs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: And these can be achieved without operating a 24/7 response unit.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We also leverage on technology in the form of noise sensors, which Members have shown a lot of interest in, to reduce the need for human officers on stakeout to catch noise as it occurs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We know that Members are eager for us to do more and scale faster.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I do want to assure Members, however, that we will do so as quickly as we can because we understand and we know how important this issue is to so many of our Members as well as the communities they represent.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: An over-reliance on CRU intervention can erode the essence of our community spirit over time, something which Dr Syed Harun very eloquently talked about.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is the case today and will continue to be the case after the establishment and roll-out of the CRU.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I spoke earlier on the enhanced mediation framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Parties who reach a mediated settlement may now register the agreement as a CDRT order, if all parties agree.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This registered settlement can then be enforced as if it were a CDRT order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the dispute must be taken to the CDRT, then the affected resident can avail himself or herself of the interim orders that we have now enhanced under the CDRT process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The evidential requirements for obtaining an interim order under the new section 5A are lower.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They should not be too hard to satisfy if the case is egregious.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is so that affected residents in those cases can avail themselves of the relief provided by the interim orders framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are serious consequences for disobeying CDRT orders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if the respondent disobeys an interim order and a CDRT order, then he can be ordered to vacate his home for a period of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is linked to the registration of settlement agreements, which I have just mentioned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Since a registered settlement agreement is enforceable like a CDRT order, repeated non-compliance can ultimately lead to an exclusion order as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Faisal Manap asked about disamenities arising from commercial units below the HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are existing processes to address such issues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But one must also bear in mind the context.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you are living and you choose to live next to a residential unit as most neighbours are, versus if you bought a unit which you know is above a commercial unit, I think the circumstances and therefore, the expectations are quite different.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And one needs to look at the different scenarios when you deal with practices and when you deal with norms between neighbours, which is what we are trying to set up in the framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Faisal Manap also suggested introducing an order for mandatory counselling sessions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: From our experience, mediation is quick and, thus far, has proven effective and our intention is to focus on increasing the uptake on mediation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mediation, as opposed to counselling, also has the benefit of being specifically focused on the issue at hand, on the parties' particular dispute and try to find consensus and common ground for that particular dispute, as opposed to a broad general counselling provision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng, Miss Rachel Ong and Mr Alex Yam raised the issue of second-hand smoke in homes and other community issues, and they asked if the CRU can address these issues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think some other Members have also accepted what I said earlier about the CRU being a very substantial endeavour and one which is going to be very broad and which is why you have heard me as well as Senior Minister of State Sim Ann say that there needs to be a calibration and we do need to have the pilot to allow us to make that calibration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But specifically on enforcement for second-hand smoke, my colleague, the Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment, Dr Amy Khor, has previously explained the Government's position on managing second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The framework here we need to think of quite carefully.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In those cases, I think Mr Louis Ng will know, there are challenges with effective enforcement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have had that debate on several occasions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The other point to bear in mind is that the framework here is designed to deal with the vast majority of disamenities between neighbours.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You have heard me say earlier the types of cases that we get and, of those, noise constitutes the vast majority.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In contrast, just a couple of weeks ago, in response to Mr Louis Ng's Parliamentary Question, Mr Louis Ng cited some numbers, but he might have forgotten that a couple of weeks ago, the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) explained to Mr Louis Ng that as a result of the measures that they have taken, the number of complaints that are second-hand smoke-related has come down.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Louis Ng remembers that, two weeks ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2021, 2022 and 2023, every year-on-year, the numbers came down.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am not saying that the problem is not there and I appreciate what Mr Louis Ng has said about the severity of second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we also need to understand the extent of the problem and what the CDMF is scoped to deal with.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this case, there are specific mechanisms that MSE has deployed with NEA to deal with second-hand smoke and, at least, from these numbers alone, they do look like there is some improvement and they will continue to work on them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The CDMF framework is designed to deal with the vast majority of disamenity cases that it is best equipped to deal with through processes like mediation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I also want to make the point to Mr Louis Ng that there were two cases that Mr Louis Ng referred to earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One was a case where he cited the individual or resident suffering a seizure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the other was a question on the order, in Mr Louis Ng's words, what purpose does this order serve if its enforcement is ineffective?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I want Mr Louis Ng to know that we had checked on these cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it does show that mediation is also effective in these cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Two, therefore, in that case, no CDRT order was issued.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is not a question of the CDRT order not being effective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, again, it is not a question of the order being ineffective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But in this case, the claimant was unable to demonstrate that there was a breach of the order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I hope that clarifies on both of those cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Alex Yam asked about the broader community-building efforts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Derrick Goh, in particular, asked about what strategies there were to increase residents' awareness of self-resolution approaches.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum made some interesting and useful suggestions on how to improve collaborative problem-solving.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, if Members heard my speech earlier, I said it is fundamental in our philosophy, even behind the CDMF, which enhances the levers for us to intervene more and to take steps upstream, that we do not lose sight of the fact that we want the community to continue to be engaged in resolving their own issues in a conciliatory and amicable way as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But in response to the Members' questions and suggestions, let me give some idea of some of the ongoing efforts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2021, MSO set up the OneService Kakis Network, or OSK Networks in short.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This network of community stakeholders works with MSO to co-create and implement ideas that address municipal issues in their own neighbourhoods and we appreciate that no two neighbourhoods are the same.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Sometimes, the needs are different, sometimes the way in which you look at disamenity might well be different, depending on the layout and the structure, size and type of the estate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, these local networks for local suggestions are useful.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, other initiatives, such as the "Love Our 'Hood Initiative" by MSO, also provide opportunities for residents and community stakeholders to develop community-based solutions to foster neighbourliness.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are also public education efforts, such as the "Then How?" Campaign by the Singapore Kindness Movement and HDB.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These efforts suggest ways for neighbours to approach one another.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One of the rate-limiting factors of mediation was the fact that neighbours did not feel that they were equipped to or that they could approach a neighbour or someone with whom they had a minor disagreement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And sometimes, because of that, then, you sort of see ghosts in the shadows and you think the worst of the situation and then the problem escalates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, these suggestions about how neighbours can approach one another, can have casual conversations and break down some barriers, allow them to ventilate and then, in turn, hear suggestions on how one can be constructive on solving the problem, are all very helpful.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MSO also partners community stakeholders, such as schools, to promote considerate behaviour through ground-up initiatives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, Dunman High School students designed standees with messages on keeping noise levels low in Jalan Batu – I think that is in Mr Lim Biow Chuan's constituency – to raise awareness of pro-social norms on quiet hours.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Temasek Polytechnic students installed LED-integrated posters in Bishan simulating traffic lights to provide visual cues on basketball court closure timings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, when you see that it is turning yellow, it means it is time to wind down and, when it is red, it is time to turn off the lights and not cause any more noise disamenity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was done to encourage basketball court users to leave before closing time, in a somewhat innovative, very casual and very non-threatening way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue to work on this to deepen social capital and encourage interaction among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Mark Lee asked about tapping on religious platforms and organisations for disputes with religious undertones.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Joan Pereira, Assoc Prof Razwana Begum and Mr Derrick Goh also asked about supporting grassroots leaders' efforts to address conflicts upstream at an earlier stage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is very much in coherence with the philosophy that we see, the CDMF.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have been, in fact, working very closely with grassroots leaders (GRLs) and agencies, such as HDB, to strengthen the existing community-based framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have said earlier that mediation is an important community-based solution that underpins the CDMF.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, what are the steps that we have taken on this?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You do not always have to go to CMC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Sometimes, the mediator can be, as I said earlier, someone residing within the community, who is senior, an elder stateman or a community or religious leader.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The plan is to have more of them trained, at least in basic mediation skills.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Should there be disputes between neighbours, they can then step in.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If these early resolution efforts fail, then authorised HDB officers will then consider the Mediation Direction, in the manner that I had outlined earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I want to just emphasise that if you receive a Mediation Direction, there is nothing wrong with that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Come, hear out your neighbour, hear out the other party.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On neighbour disputes that involve religious matters, the IRCCs, now known as Harmony Circles, provide assistance to frontline agencies as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have worked hard over the years to build up that social capital and trust amongst our different communities; our Harmony Circles have also been refreshed and energised with members that have a broader network to reach out to a broader segment of the community.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As part of our efforts to strengthen the CDMF, MCCY has identified selected Harmony Circle members to attend basic mediation training together with PA's grassroots leaders as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will, in turn, strengthen their ability to provide ground support when needed for religion-related disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These, sometimes, if you do not quickly fix it or address it, can have the potential to become highly inflammatory, very emotive and it is not wise to have them escalate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members also raised several questions on promoting the use of community mediation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling, in particular, asked about our efforts to encourage greater participation in CMC mediation and how the Government will evaluate its effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Derrick Goh and Mr Alex Yam spoke about enhancing accessibility.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
